title: Finanzmärkte im Wandel: KI, Staatsschulden, Energie: Was treibt die Welt?
summary: Sabine Mauderer sees three calls on capital appearing together: AI infrastructure, public borrowing and the energy system that both households and new technologies need. In her BlackRock Leader Circle speech she argues that this combination could change financing conditions over a longer horizon. Governments require money for infrastructure, defence, digitalisation and climate policy while companies are increasing investment. That would mark a change from an environment characterised by high savings and comparatively weak investment demand. A rise in the cost of finance is conditional on demand for capital remaining stronger over time. She supplies neither a target for bond yields nor a date by which competition for funds must raise them.

The scale of AI spending is central to the argument. Mauderer cites an OECD estimate that nine large technology companies could invest around $4 trillion cumulatively by 2030. The figure concerns possible expenditure by the companies. It cannot be read as their prospective bond issuance. Data centres, advanced chips and the energy infrastructure they require are large up-front commitments. Technology groups had been able to finance much of their spending internally. Bond finance is now becoming more important, extending the set of investors exposed to that spending beyond equity owners.

Europe participates in this financing even when the investment decision is taken in the United States. Mauderer cites more than €50 billion of outstanding euro-denominated bonds issued by major US technology firms and Meta’s first euro issue of €9 billion. The first figure describes a stock across borrowers; the second describes one financing transaction. Neither indicates how much new debt a particular project will require. Expectations about earnings embedded in technology valuations also matter. AI could increase productivity, enable new business models and benefit European industrial users, yet the pace at which investment delivers earnings remains unknown. As recent US price declines illustrated for the speaker, changing expectations can produce a repricing with consequences beyond technology equities.

In sovereign debt markets, Mauderer sees several plausible explanations for higher long-term yields: expected growth and inflation, monetary policy, public finances and term premiums. The speech does not allocate the move among them. Central banks are gradually reducing their bond holdings, making private investors more important in absorbing supply. She welcomes a greater private role while warning that leveraged investors can amplify price changes and reduce liquidity when markets are already stressed. Sovereign yields then transmit the tightening to a broader range of borrowing costs because they provide a benchmark for other issuers.

Energy connects the financing argument to the macroeconomy on two horizons. A geopolitical disruption can push up energy prices, reducing household spending power and raising business costs. Inflation can rise as growth slows; changes in the expected policy response can feed into bond yields. Over the longer run, wider AI deployment needs sufficient electricity generation, reliable supply and networks that can deliver power to data centres. Investment demand therefore extends beyond chips and software. For European industry, reliable energy at an affordable price affects where production can take place. Mauderer sees scope for Europe’s existing savings, industrial base and innovative firms to support productive investment, provided markets can connect them. She does not identify which companies will capture the returns or which segment of the yield curve will absorb the financing pressure.

questions.question: What fraction of prospective AI spending would require external financing?
questions.detail: The OECD number concerns cumulative investment; observed euro bonds show that external funding already matters. Neither establishes future net issuance. For a credit supply view, compare each issuer’s capital expenditure, operating cash flow, distributions, debt maturities and intended funding currency using accounts and prospectuses. Refinancing and genuinely incremental borrowing have different implications for private investors’ absorption capacity.

questions.question: Which evidence would distinguish competition for capital from a change in expected policy?
questions.detail: Mauderer lists several reasons for higher sovereign yields, while the competition argument depends on sustained demand. Compare issuance by maturity net of redemptions and central-bank holdings with changes in the expected policy path and alternative term-premium estimates. Debt-management announcements and central-bank holdings data would help judge whether long-duration supply has actually increased relative to demand.

questions.question: Which electricity constraints delay project cash flows, and who bears the cost?
questions.detail: The speech links AI expansion to generation and grids but gives no project-level evidence on the binding constraint. Examine grid connection queues, contracted power availability, tariff arrangements and the allocation of upgrade costs in utility and technology-company filings. Returns can differ substantially between a data-centre operator that secures a connection and a supplier that must finance the network ahead of revenue.
